title: The Signs That Took the Shine
markdown:
The park was a beautiful patchwork of green grass and bright colours, Uncle Theo's favourite place. His kind hands worked wonders in the soil, helping petunias grow so soft and bright they looked like they were painted by a rainbow. They bloomed in swathes of rosy pinks, deep purples, and sunny yellows, each one placed like a precious jewel.

Poppy the squirrel lived in the grand old oak tree at the park's edge. Her bushy tail would twitch with a thousand thoughts when she was busy, which was always. She made sure her nest was very neat, polishing each acorn until it shone like a tiny brown star. Not far away, Jun the mole, with cheeks as rosy as apples and a nose that wiggled at the smell of damp earth, had dug tunnels that his neighbours underground all talked about.

This year, the park had a new, special addition. Young Timmy, the junior groundskeeper, had a very unusual skill. He could make signs. And these weren't just any signs. Timmy's signs were wonderfully clear, simply drawn, and quite charming. Their lines were perfectly straight, as if drawn by a ruler made of sunshine, and each one had a friendly little curl at the bottom, like a polite little wave.

"Please Mind the Daisies," one sign declared, its letters so neat and clean they seemed to hum a happy tune. Another, near the calm pond, gently announced, "Gentle Ducks Enjoy Quiet Paddles." And right there, tucked among Uncle Theo’s prize petunias, a sign stood proudly: "These Blossoms Flourish with Care."

Uncle Theo, who loved quiet moments, loved the whisper of leaves, the buzz of busy bees, and the simple, everyday wonder of a flower opening to the sun. He spent his days tending his garden, carefully pulling weeds, patiently watering, and helping every plant grow its best.

One bright afternoon, a lady wearing a hat the colour of a canary stopped by Uncle Theo’s petunias. She pointed at the sign. "Oh, how lovely!" she exclaimed, her voice like little bells. "These blossoms do flourish with care! What a thoughtful sign."

Uncle Theo, with his watering can in hand, gave a small, happy smile. He had cared, after all.

But then, more people started to stop.

"This pond is so peaceful," a gentleman murmured, looking at the sign that read, "Gentle Ducks Enjoy Quiet Paddles." He stroked his chin. "Whoever put this up really understands peacefulness."

A little girl, her pigtails bouncing, skipped past the daisy patch, her finger pointing. "Look, Mummy! 'Please Mind the Daisies'! They're so pretty, we mustn't step on them!"

And so it went. Soon, it seemed, everyone in the park was praising the signs. They would admire the perfect letters, the clear, helpful words, and the very polite tone.

Poppy, from her leafy home in the old oak, watched it all happen. Her tail began to twitch, a sure sign she was thinking hard. "Jun," she chattered, her voice a worried little squeak, "have you noticed what's going on?"

Jun popped his head out of a newly dug hole, his whiskers quivering with curiosity. "Noticed what, Poppy?" he asked, his voice muffled by the earth. "That these carrots I’ve just found are extra crunchy? Because they really are!"

"No, no, not the carrots!" Poppy scampered down the trunk to be closer. "It’s Uncle Theo! People look at his beautiful flowers, yes, but then they say, 'What a wonderful sign!' They aren't saying, 'What wonderful flowers!' or 'What wonderful gardening!'"

Jun tilted his head, his rosy cheeks puffing out. "But the signs are very nice," he admitted. Then he paused, thinking. "They are quite clear, aren't they? They tell you exactly what to do."

"Exactly!" chirped Poppy. "But Uncle Theo does all the real work. The signs just… stand there!" A tiny puff of annoyance escaped her.

Poppy and Jun, a determined pair, decided a little bit of investigation was needed. They would look into these attention-grabbing signs.

Meanwhile, Uncle Theo, his straw hat shading his thoughtful face, was starting to feel like a forgotten bloom in his own garden. He loved his park, of course, but a small word of praise for his careful weeding, a compliment on his perfectly turned compost, would have been so nice. He had spent many, many hours helping those petunias, making sure each soft petal opened just right. And all anyone seemed to notice was the polite little sign nearby.

The next morning, Poppy and Jun found a cosy hiding spot behind a big, leafy rhododendron bush and started to watch. A family walked past. The father stopped right in front of the "Please Mind the Daisies" sign. "Very clear," he said, adjusting his glasses that sat on his nose. "Such nice writing. Young Timmy is a real artist, don't you think?"

The mother nodded happily. "And so polite! I feel I must tread as carefully as a mouse!"

Jun whispered, his voice barely a sound, "They don't even seem to see the daisies, Poppy! They're looking at the words!"

Poppy’s tail puffed out like a tiny, furry explosion. "It's like they're thanking the words for being nice, not Uncle Theo for making the flowers nice enough to need minding!"

They kept watching as people admired the "Gentle Ducks Enjoy Quiet Paddles" sign, while the ducks themselves, plump and happy, waddled by, completely unnoticed. The signs were made so perfectly, so invitingly clear, that they had, it seemed, become the main stars of the park.

Poppy and Jun watched all afternoon. They saw people pointing, admiring, and, yes, thanking the signs. The signs were so well made, they were almost too good. They had become so polite and clear, they had politely and clearly taken all the attention away from the park itself, and most importantly, from Uncle Theo’s hard work.

Then, a small, sad idea started to grow in Uncle Theo’s mind. He found a small, smooth piece of wood and, dipping a fine twig into a little bit of berry juice, he carefully painted a tiny sign. It read, in his shaky, from-the-heart writing: "These Petunias Cherish Your Kind Eyes." He gently placed it right in the middle of his most beautiful, soft petunia.

Poppy and Jun watched from their hiding place, their little hearts sinking lower and lower. A few moments later, a woman with a very big, very colourful hat stopped. She looked at Uncle Theo's sign. "Oh, how sweet!" she cooed, her voice like a gentle breeze. "This sign is so charming! 'Your Kind Eyes'! What a lovely, lovely thought." She smiled at the sign, then walked away, her eyes still fixed on the polite, painted words.

Uncle Theo sighed, a sound as soft as leaves rustling in autumn. He felt even more forgotten than before. The park, which usually buzzed with happy activity and cheerful chatter, felt a little quieter now, a little less bright. He felt forgotten. This was despair, he realised.

Poppy and Jun scurried over to sit beside Uncle Theo. He was gently trimming a stray leaf from a rose bush, his shoulders slumped. "It's like nobody sees me," he murmured, his voice thick with sadness. "Or my flowers. Just the signs."

Poppy nudged him gently with her nose. "But we see you, Uncle Theo," she said, her voice soft and comforting. "And we see your flowers. They are the very best flowers in the whole wide world."

Jun nodded hard, his little nose wiggling with pure happiness. "They smell like sunshine and joy!" he added, his voice full of feeling.

They sat in comfortable quiet for a moment, the silence broken only by the distant, happy chirping of birds. Uncle Theo managed a small, shaky smile. It was so good to have friends who truly saw him.

But seeing, Poppy and Jun realised, wasn't quite enough. Something needed to be done, something to help everyone else see too. Poppy, with her quick and clever mind, and Jun, with his strong and capable paws, put their heads together. "We need to remind everyone," Poppy declared, her voice full of determination, "that the signs are just telling us about the wonderful things Uncle Theo has made."

They decided to help Uncle Theo in a very special way. Poppy, with her nimble paws, busily collected fallen leaves in shades of russet and gold, and tiny, colourful petals that had drifted from the blossoms. Jun, with his excellent digging skills, created a soft, welcoming bed of the richest earth. Together, they helped Uncle Theo arrange his most beautiful flowers in a prominent spot right near the park entrance, where everyone would see them.

Then, they found a large, smooth, grey stone, worn smooth by time and the elements. With more berry juice and a fine-tipped twig, they helped Uncle Theo paint a truly special message. This wasn't a polite instruction like Timmy's signs. This was a thank you, painted with love and heartfelt truthfulness. It read: "Thank you for noticing. These flowers bloom because of care."

They placed the stone and the vibrant floral arrangement where many people would see them as they entered the park.

The next morning, as the park began to fill with its usual happy visitors, people approached, their eyes immediately drawn to the bright, welcoming blooms and the simple, heartfelt stone. They paused. They read.

A little boy, instead of rushing towards the "Please Mind the Daisies" sign, ran directly to Uncle Theo, who was gently tending to his roses. "Mr. Theo," he exclaimed, his voice loud and clear, "your flowers are so pretty! And this stone says thank you for noticing! I do notice!" He pointed excitedly to the magnificent petunias. "They're the best!"

Soon, others followed his lead. People began to look from the signs to the flowers, from the flowers to the stone, and then, their eyes finding Uncle Theo as he worked, they began to thank him.

"Oh, Uncle Theo, your roses are simply magnificent!"

"These petunias are truly glorious!"

"Thank you for making our park so beautiful and welcoming."

Uncle Theo's smile spread across his face, as bright and warm as the midday sun. His straw hat seemed to sit a little straighter, and his eyes sparkled with newfound joy.

Poppy, watching from her cosy spot in the oak tree, felt a deep, contented twitch in her bushy tail. Jun, peeking out from his hole, wiggled his nose with pure happiness. The park, it seemed, had found its happy balance again. The signs were still clear and friendly, but now, everyone remembered to thank the gardener, too.
characters: Poppy the squirrel, Jun the mole, Uncle Theo
